sources.text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is “transitioning out” of her role, multiple sources and a senior White House official told ABC News on Friday.
Zacharia started as press secretary on Monday.
President Donald Trump earlier Friday told reporters he asked Zacharia to reconsider whether she wants to stay in the position.
“I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider,"” Trump said.
“I said, ‘Katie, you know, you don’t have to do this if you don’t want,"” the president said. “She said, ‘This is a lot tougher.’ I said, ‘Welcome to the world of Trump."”

sources.news_title: Trump drops his new press secretary after a week of controversy
sources.text:
Katie Zacharia will leave her post as White House press secretary just five days after taking it up, according to advisers to President Donald Trump quoted by several US media outlets, following a widely criticised first briefing and the revelation that she had presented herself as a lawyer without passing the bar exam.
A White House official said Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the role. Before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia, Trump told reporters he had suggested she reconsider staying on: “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. Katie, do you need this?” The president said she had been treated “very unfairly” by the media and that many people wanted the job.
Zacharia, appointed on October 9 to succeed Karoline Leavitt, held her first and only briefing on Tuesday, lasting 14 minutes, in which she was unable to answer a question about whether the United States had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Days later she admitted that, although she graduated in law, she had not passed the bar exam, despite presenting herself as a lawyer for years.
Her tenure is shorter than the 11 days Anthony Scaramucci spent as Trump’s communications director in 2017.

The tumultuous tenure of White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has already come to an end just three days after her first press briefing.
After his new hire shambled her way through yet another Fox News appearance the night before, President Donald Trump said on Friday that he'd suggested Zacharia "reconsider" her role as the top White House spokesperson.
"Maybe it's not for her," Trump said, suggesting Zacharia may continue working for him “in some form, but maybe a more pleasant form.”
Zacharia, who stepped into the role formerly held by Karoline Leavitt, lasted a total of five days in the job. That's less than half the tenure of Anthony Scaramucci—who departed his role as White House communications director after just 11 days during Trump's first term.
Her qualifications were in doubt from the moment Trump plucked her from an obscure role as a Fox News commentator for the highly visible job. Journalists dug up old posts in which she promoted the QAnon and Pizzagate conspiracies, as well as Trump's false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.
From the start of Zacharia's disastrous briefing on Tuesday, many observers predicted it could also be her last.
She was relentlessly panned after struggling to read through her fully scripted remarks (and at one point accidentally referring to her husband as "my president"). She cut the briefing short after just 14 minutes, taking only three questions, all from right-wing outlets.
It also became clear that, despite Trump's introduction of her as "an attorney," she'd never actually passed the bar exam and had misrepresented her credentials for years.
Asked by reporters earlier this week in which state she had passed the bar exam, she said, “When I moved to China" before later claiming not to have heard the question.
Even Fox News host Sean Hannity—a longtime Trump loyalist—challenged her explanation, confronting her Thursday with a report documenting “15 social media posts where you identify yourself as an attorney.”
“I think they were retweets,” Zacharia replied, arguing to a flummoxed Hannity that sharing the posts did not constitute endorsing the title.
While Zacharia's inability to do damage control appeared to do her in, Democratic strategist Mike Nellis emphasized that the problem was not her dishonesty—a trait that is practically a prerequisite to serve in the Trump administration.
"Katie Zacharia wasn't fired because she lied," Nellis wrote on social media. "It was because she was a bad liar. It's a key distinction.”
To some, Zacharia's tenure represented a disastrous culmination of Trump's willingness to eschew competence and experience for personal flattery and undying loyalty when appointing officials during his second term.
Zacharia said she got on Trump's radar by scheduling her TV appearances when she knew he'd be watching.
While other advisers questioned the pick, Zacharia's appointment was reportedly championed by Natalie Harp, Trump’s ever-present personal assistant and a fellow blonde conservative television personality.

"She looks nice for him," said former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Steele on MS NOW. "She fits his idea of the blonde white female standing at that podium publicly pronouncing his noise in a way that makes him, when he's watching it, feel good."
Steele emphasized that with just weeks left before a midterm election widely viewed as a referendum on Trump, "the White House is voiceless."
"They do not have a press secretary in place," he said, "because the president picked an incompetent individual to do the job."
Though very few seemed to think Zacharia could turn things around, she did have one person in her corner—perhaps the only other person who could possibly understand her experience: Scaramucci.
While others bet she would not even last "one Scaramucci," The Mooch himself predicted—even after her disastrous Hannity appearance on Thursday—that "she will make it. I have the over."
Following news on Friday that she did not, in fact, make it, Scaramucci wrote: "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

sources.news_title: The Five-Day Press Secretary
Trump’s Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Leaves Job After Five Days
sources.text:
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was pushed out Friday after less than a week in the high-profile job, following a series of blunders that added to distractions for her embattled boss President Donald Trump.
“Can confirm,” a White House official told AFP, after Fox News reported that Zacharia, 41, was “transitioning out.”
The writing was on the wall earlier when Trump made clear he was ready to see his newly minted spokeswoman go amid criticism that she had pretended to be a lawyer and over her one, much-mocked press briefing.
“I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?,'” Trump told reporters. “I said, ‘Katie, you don’t have to do this’… I said to her, ‘Honestly if I were you I’d reconsider.'”
Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.
Zacharia had got off to a rocky start with her debut press room briefing Tuesday morning.
It lasted less than 15 minutes, beginning with a remarkably slow reading out of what she said were Trump’s many accomplishments — then taking just three questions from journalists.
She then was plunged into controversy when it emerged that her previous claims to be a lawyer were not true.
The kerfuffle is a distraction for 80-year-old Trump as he flies around the country trying to boost Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections, with polls predicting a drubbing.
The Republican leader himself also faces ever-lower polls as Americans sour over the war against Iran, inflation and perceptions of corruption.
Not a real lawyer
Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
While she does have a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged Thursday she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practicing law in the United States.
She embarked on a series of damage-control interviews on Trump-friendly outlets, but they did no good.
In one of them, Fox News’ Sean Hannity, a close Trump ally, appeared dismissive of Zacharia.
He asked the press secretary if she ever retook the bar exam. She replied: “I did not.”
“It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” she said.
In another interview Thursday with pro-Trump outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was “distracted and overwhelmed” by plans to move to China with her husband.
Zacharia said “many people in the field” had assured her that she could “label myself a lawyer,” given her law degree.
China’s toilets
“Fox and Friends,” which often conducts friendly interviews with Trump administration officials, was unusually direct Friday when a host asked Zacharia if she still had the confidence of the president.
“I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me,” she said, sidestepping the question.
Zacharia further stirred controversy on Thursday when she disparaged China, whose leader Xi Jinping was recently Trump’s guest in a pomp-filled Washington visit.
The press secretary recalled the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the United States.
“I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,'” she told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded Friday that Zacharia should “visit China more often.”
AFP

sources.news_title: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
sources.text:
Analysis: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.
These were not the best of circumstances.
Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
In just five days, she was out – the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.
The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered – in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day.
"Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."
He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".
In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.
Trump may be wondering whether Zacharia "needs" the press secretary job, but presidents – including this one - benefit most from a competent press secretary in times of crisis.
And while there may not be an immediate crisis, this White House is certainly facing growing adversity.
Across the US, Republican candidates are scrambling to hold on to their seats in the upcoming elections. Some are doing so by distancing themselves from the president and his policies, creating new stresses and faultlines within a party that has for so long been broadly unified behind Trump.
Meanwhile, the White House has been beset by a series of controversies – including allegations of corruption that forced the resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and an abrupt reversal of plans to publicly air a military execution in December after widespread bipartisan backlash.
A skilled press secretary may have been able to navigate these political landmines while continuing to push out the White House's preferred message in the face of a building media frenzy.
Karoline Leavitt, who worked as Trump's press secretary from the start of his second term until she resigned in August a few months after welcoming her second child, proved highly adept at defending the administration from the press room lectern while avoiding stumbles and maintaining a collegial relationship with journalists.
Her performance set a high bar for Zacharia, who was a relative novice. It was a mark she failed to reach or even approach, although she never really had much of a chance.
The speed at which she failed was astounding, setting a modern record for the shortest-tenured White House press secretary.
Zacharia's halting Tuesday press conference performance, combined with those questions about her legal background, essentially sealed her fate.
And subsequent press appearances, including a less-than-welcoming interview with conservative pundit Sean Hannity on Thursday – which Trump said he watched – did nothing to change that.
As president, Trump has essentially acted as his own press secretary, making major announcements and changing policies from the Oval Office, the White House lawn, airfield tarmacs – wherever he happens to be.
Zacharia herself noted this phenomenon prior to being tabbed for the White House job. "President Trump does not need a spokesperson," she posted on X. "He is his own best press secretary."
Now, he will have to be.
Trump's penchant for speaking off the cuff, however, has made the job a difficult one over the course of his two terms in office.
His press secretaries have sometimes had their public statements undermined by presidential pronouncements. At other times, they've been left out of the loop of key decisions.
When they have been effective, they have managed to ride the choppier waves while also smoothing relations with the media - providing context for inquisitive journalists and helping tamp down any simmering issues.
In comments to Fox News on Friday, Trump said that he is in "no rush" to find a new press secretary. But at such a critical time in his second term, Trump will be without the help that someone like Leavitt offered so consistently.
He may come to regret not having it.

sources.news_title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after just five days
sources.text:
WASHINGTON | Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job.
Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice.
Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaotic nature of Zacharia’s appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president’s first term, which had largely been absent from his second.
In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press.
“I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,'” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.'”
Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House did not respond to a request for confirmation.
In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, “‘Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,'” and that he wanted “her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.”
The president said he’d make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, “When I get back, we’re gonna talk.” He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job.
Zacharia’s first official day on the job was Monday
In Zacharia’s first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also wouldn’t say when her next press briefing might be.
Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer
Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China.
That was part of the unusual amount of skepticism that Zacharia faced from those friendly to the administration, including Fox News host Sean Hannity, who pressed the new White House spokeswoman on why she wasn’t forthcoming about her professional background.
Hannity, known to be friendly with Trump, asked Zacharia after she confirmed she did not pass the bar exam in California, “Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine law school and then took a different career path and I took the bar once and didn’t pass it?'”
“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?” he asked. “Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction. Why didn’t you just say, ‘I never practiced law?'”
Zacharia reiterated to Hannity that she wasn’t acting as a lawyer nor offering legal advice. And she said Friday during that Fox News interview that she wasn’t asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary. Both she and Trump have said she was hired to work in press and communications, not as an administration lawyer.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president’s social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration.
Price reported from Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia.

In this edition of Party Animals: Bret Baier first moved to Washington in the wake of 9/11, having been tasked by Fox News with reporting from outside the burning Pentagon. Now he’s the anchor of Special Report, the network’s flagship news program, and a star in Trump’s turbulent Washington. Last week I grabbed dinner with the anchorman at a Georgetown restaurant he calls his “clubhouse.” Over surf-and-turf, we discussed the evolution of Fox News, what he makes of his colleagues on the opinion side of the network, and his hot-and-cold relationship with the president.

In the Loop:
Press Enclosure
It was a big week for Katie Zacharia, Trump’s new press secretary. When she took the podium for her first briefing on Tuesday, the little-known MAGA surrogate was nervous. Her briefing lasted just a few minutes. She answered three questions and then awkwardly darted out of the room.
On Friday afternoon, Trump delivered an ominous verdict: “I said [to] Katie, ‘You know, you don’t have to do this if you don’t want to,’” he said, adding that she’d been treated “nastily” so far. “I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’”
Within minutes, The New York Times reported that Zacharia was out. She lasted five days, four if you count Columbus Day as a holiday—less than half a Scaramucci, in Trump West Wing parlance. A White House official confirmed her ouster to Party Animals.
The administration had been in damage control mode ever since her first briefing. In a statement afterward, the White House called her performance “powerful.” Communications director Steven Cheung said that she “commanded the room.” But in an edited video put out by the White House that showed her march to the podium, set to pickup-truck-commercial music, Zacharia appeared visibly fearful.
It was just the beginning. After the briefing, as she accompanied Trump to Marine One, New York Times reporter Shawn McCreesh asked Trump in which state Zacharia had passed the bar. The president turned to his new aide, who identifies as a lawyer. “When I moved to China,” she said. What? The Wall Street Journal later reported that Zacharia received a JD but didn’t pass the bar. Zacharia subsequently told McCreesh that she had misheard his question (this can happen over the din of Marine One) and thought he had asked, “Where were you after law school?”
Then, on Thursday night, Zacharia appeared on Fox News for an interview with Sean Hannity, who surprised viewers by pummeling the new Trump aide with questions over her short debut briefing and claims about her lawyerly background. After a rough week, many in the White House began asking whether Zacharia would last. But they weren’t ready to give up yet. In a statement to Party Animals on Thursday, Cheung called Zacharia a “fabulous and wonderful addition to the team.”
The Execution Will Not Be Livestreamed
Trump has announced that the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood attacker will not air publicly. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced last week (in an interview with Pizzagate conspiracist Jack Posobiec) that the Pentagon would air the execution of the man convicted of the attack that killed 13 and wounded 30 more. The idea of livestreaming the shooting of bullets into a wheelchair-bound paraplegic was quickly met with bipartisan resistance, and Trump and Vice President JD Vance backed away from it almost immediately. One poll found that a whopping 80% of Americans opposed the plan. On Thursday, Trump announced that the execution will not, in fact, be streamed. He reasoned that “very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”

White House press secretary Zacharia fired in less than a week after facing criticism
WASHINGTON - White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump's top spokesperson.
Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to two separate White House officials. She faced days of questions about her legal credentials and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews.
The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger just over two weeks before November's midterm elections, a critical period when the president is seeking to tout his administration's accomplishments and help his fellow Republicans retain control of Congress.
Trump told reporters earlier on Friday that he had asked Zacharia to reconsider whether to continue in her role after facing tough press coverage during her first days on the job.
"I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a weekend trip.
He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he intended to revisit the conversation with Zacharia later.
Zacharia started on Monday and held her debut White House briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the press secretary role on October 7 and was offered the job to succeed Karoline Leavitt a week ago.
She soon faced questions about her career, which she said included a tenure practicing law. Trump had also described her as an attorney.
"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in an emailed statement on Wednesday.
Reuters could not find records showing the Pepperdine University law school graduate was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any US state or the District of Columbia.
During a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she did not pass the barexam. Law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.
Zacharia and the White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment about her firing.
Earlier on Friday, she told reporters at the White House that she was looking forward to working with the press.
Trump hired Zacharia after expressing concerns about the media coverage of his administration, feeling he needed a new spokesperson who could amplify his achievements, according to two people familiar with the conversations.
In a phone interview with Fox on Friday, Trump said he was in no rush to name a new press secretary.

For Zacharia, the transition ends a brief and highly publicized period as the president’s chief spokesperson.
For President Trump, the immediate task is selecting another press secretary capable of representing his administration during a demanding election season.

sources.news_title: Scaramucci replaced by shorter unit of time - a Zacharia
sources.text:
A Scaramucci has often been used as a tongue-in-cheek measure of time in politics, particularly in the Trump era.
It refers to Anthony Scaramucci's brief tenure as White House communications director in July 2017, when he lasted just 11 days.
But now, it has been replaced by a new, shorter unit of time: the Zacharia.
Katie Zacharia was "let go" as White House press secretary just five days into the job. That's less than half the time Anthony Scaramucci lasted in 2017.
Just last Friday, news broke at the White House that she had been offered the role. Many of us had noted how much of an outsider she was, who had not been tipped as a potential candidate.

These briefings can usually go on for an hour.

Another said they felt sorry for her.
Almost immediately, people in the room began speculating about how long she would last.
The writing appeared to be on the wall.
It just wasn't good enough.

He was giving her the benefit of the doubt.

Controversy began to swirl when questions arose about whether she had passed the US bar exam, a requirement for practising law.
An ethics watchdog filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association on Wednesday seeking an investigation into claims that she is a lawyer.

But I was drinking and we got a beautiful husband and family. I meant the family as today," the transcript reads. "And I said, you should drink it. Because you don't want to go through it."

I'll talk to her tonight or tomorrow. Like I said, I think you should drink it instead." The transcript as aired by ABC News is difficult to follow in places, but the president's comments came as he was leaving the White House and being asked about the press secretary's status.
NBC News reported that earlier Friday, before the departure news broke, Trump said he would let Zacharia decide whether to remain as his press secretary after he suggested she was treated harshly by the media during her first week on the job.
"She's been treated, I would say pretty nastily, and I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want," Trump said, according to NBC News.
The outlet reported Trump also said that if he were in her shoes, he would "reconsider" and said he would be having a conversation with her later about her situation.

The president's quick elevation of Zacharia from conservative media commentator to the high-profile White House job was itself a surprise, NBC News reported. The president announced her appointment on Friday, and she gave her first briefing on Tuesday morning, right after a three-day holiday weekend.
The story has been taken up widely beyond the outlets that broke it. The New York Times reported that the ouster came as Zacharia was shadowed by questions about how she had presented her legal career and handled her first press briefing. Fox News reported that Zacharia has been fired as White House press secretary.
CNN Business reported that Zacharia's firing was foreshadowed by a chilly Fox News reception, and that her first week was all about Katie Zacharia when the role should have been about the president and his agenda. The Guardian, in a live blog, noted that five days on the job would make Zacharia the shortest-serving press secretary, and that a White House official confirmed to the outlet she is "transitioning out" from the role.
The Guardian also pointed to recent reporting as context for the news.
Among the items NBC News listed in its coverage was an item stating that China invited Katie Zacharia to visit more often after she said it lacks "proper toilets."
The underlying claim that Zacharia is leaving the role is being reported on the strength of sourcing at NBC News, ABC News, Fox News, The New York Times, CNN Business and The Guardian, and is being described by those outlets as what sources are telling them. President Trump's own comments as aired by ABC News came before the departure was reported.
Next News Network could not independently verify the claim that Zacharia is leaving the White House press secretary role.
The accounts carrying the story span broadcast networks, cable news and print outlets: NBC News, ABC News, Fox News, The New York Times, CNN Business and The Guardian. ABC News' post included the on-camera comments from the president and Scott's reporting from the White House.
Our Take
Five days is not a tenure. It is a news cycle. And the fact that a White House press secretary can be elevated from conservative media commentator to the podium and then escorted out again inside a single week tells you something about how the modern press operation is treated by the people who run it and how it is treated by the people who cover it.
Look at what the president himself said, as aired by ABC News. He told reporters he had already told Zacharia she did not have to do the job. He said he would let her decide whether to stay. He said he would talk to her that night or the next day. That is a president publicly leaving his own press secretary twisting, and he did it before the departure was even reported.
The media did what it always does. It made the week about the person instead of the message. CNN Business said as much out loud, noting that her first week was all about Katie Zacharia when the role should have been about the president and his agenda. That is a rare admission from an industry that spent the week doing exactly that.
The bar exam question is a fair one. If you present yourself as a lawyer, you should be able to show the license. But fair questions do not require a five-day execution, and the same outlets that howled about the short tenure had already written the obituary before she finished her first briefing.
The conservative movement gained nothing from this. It lost a voice on the podium. The establishment press gained a scalp, and it will spend the weekend telling you it was all about qualifications. Five days. Remember that number the next time they tell you they just want competent people in the briefing room.

sources.news_title: Katie Zacharia Fired: Her Biography, Trump Ties and Successor Search
sources.text:
Katie Zacharia was dismissed as President Donald Trump’s White House press secretary on October 16, ending a five-day tenure dominated by questions about her legal credentials and public descriptions of her professional background.
A White House official confirmed her dismissal to Reuters.
Trump announced her selection on October 9; she began work on October 12 and delivered her first briefing the following day.
Her departure followed an acknowledgment that she had never passed the bar examination, despite Trump introducing her as an attorney. Before confirmation of her dismissal, the president told reporters he had encouraged her to reconsider whether she wanted the job.
Katie Zacharia’s biography: California, Pepperdine and China
Zacharia, 41, entered the White House with experience in conservative television, university fundraising, political advocacy and communications for Trump’s media company.
Pepperdine University confirms that she earned an undergraduate degree in 2007 and a law degree in 2011. Her undergraduate field was political science. While attending law school, she interned in the White House during George W. Bush’s presidency and worked as a research assistant to law professor Jim Gash, now Pepperdine’s president.
Her career subsequently took her to Beijing. According to her LinkedIn employment history, examined by The Washington Post, she worked on the international practice team at Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013. The White House defended that experience as work on international transactions, but did not provide evidence that she held an American law license.
Zacharia later returned to Pepperdine, serving as director of development for special projects from 2023 to 2025. The university also identifies her as a member of its law school’s Dean’s Council. Its appointment announcement, citing her LinkedIn profile, listed an earlier general counsel role at Fix California, the conservative organization founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell.
She became a recurring television commentator, appearing on Fox News, Newsmax and One America News. She is married to Tyler Zacharia and has four children; her family’s California residence became an issue during an earlier Washington assignment.
She briefly served in the Department of Homeland Security’s public affairs operation in 2026. In a March 31 departure announcement, she expressed support for Trump’s immigration policies and the work of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She said regular travel between Washington and California had placed a strain on her family.
She subsequently became a senior communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group, the company behind Truth Social. That provided a direct professional connection to the president’s business interests before she became his government spokeswoman.
Her route to the press secretary’s office also involved television appearances. In an interview before her dismissal, Zacharia said she watched Trump’s social media activity to identify the subjects occupying his attention, then discussed those subjects on air. She described those appearances as an audition for the position.
The Guardian reported that a White House official contacted her on October 7 and asked her to travel from Los Angeles to Washington. She met Trump and accepted the position on October 9.
Zacharia said she had sought advice about her qualifications and understood that she could describe herself as a lawyer, while avoiding “attorney” or “esquire.”
The legal credentials controversy
The dispute concerned the difference between earning a law degree and obtaining authorization to practice law.
Reuters reported that it could not find a record of Zacharia’s bar membership in any American state or the District of Columbia. On October 15, she acknowledged in a Fox News interview that she had failed the California bar examination in 2011 and had not taken it again.
Her account of working in China also attracted questions about what duties she performed and under what credentials. The White House maintained that she had appropriate qualifications for her international transactional work.
Her first briefing on October 13 lasted approximately 14 minutes. She directed reporters to question Trump himself later that day. The Associated Press’s account of her debut described renewed debate over how much substantive information the office should provide when the president frequently speaks directly to reporters.
The 10 press secretaries before Zacharia
In reverse chronological order, the preceding officeholders served three presidents:
- Karoline Leavitt — Trump, 2025–2026. A former Trump White House assistant press secretary and 2024 campaign spokeswoman, Leavitt became the youngest person appointed to the position, at 27. She departed in August 2026.
Leavitt publicly supported Zacharia’s appointment on October 9. In an X post reproduced in coverage of the announcement, she wrote: “Katie has my full support and I will be cheering for her and the entire team at the White House every day.” Leavitt also expressed confidence that Zacharia would serve Trump and the country well. This was an endorsement of her appointment, issued a week before the dismissal. I found no verified subsequent statement from Leavitt withdrawing that support or discussing the firing.
- Karine Jean-Pierre — Joe Biden, 2022–2025. Previously Biden’s principal deputy press secretary, she became the first Black person and first openly gay person to hold the office.
Jean-Pierre criticized Zacharia’s preparation and the brevity of her first briefing during an October 13 CNN appearance. According to CNN’s transcript, she said: “You cannot just go in there not prepared. And so, what I saw today was odd.” Jean-Pierre said she had spent four hours preparing with her team each day as press secretary. She contrasted Zacharia’s appearance of less than 15 minutes, with only a few questions, with her own briefings lasting 40 to 60 minutes. Her criticism preceded the dismissal; I found no verified comment from her about the removal itself.
- Jen Psaki — Biden, 2021–2022. An Obama administration communications veteran and former State Department spokeswoman, Psaki later entered television broadcasting.
Psaki mocked Zacharia’s October 13 debut in an X post quoted by the Associated Press: “Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit….except it wasnt.” The remark referred to the briefing, rather than Zacharia’s legal credentials or eventual dismissal. I found no verified statement from Psaki specifically reacting to the firing in the material reviewed.
- Kayleigh McEnany — Trump, 2020–2021. A Harvard Law School graduate and former Republican National Committee spokeswoman, she served during the coronavirus pandemic and the 2020 election.
McEnany offered a more sympathetic assessment of Zacharia’s preparation time. The Wall Street Journal’s reporting quoted her as saying Zacharia had “very little runway” before facing reporters.
- Stephanie Grisham — Trump, 2019–2020. Previously Melania Trump’s spokeswoman, Grisham held the press secretary’s title without conducting a formal White House press briefing.
Grisham questioned how thoroughly Trump had considered the appointment. In an interview quoted by The Bulwark, she suggested that Trump might have offered Zacharia the position during a meeting without extensive consultation or vetting.
- Sarah Huckabee Sanders — Trump, 2017–2019. A campaign aide and deputy press secretary before her promotion, Sanders later became governor of Arkansas.
- Sean Spicer — Trump, 2017. A former Republican National Committee communications director, Spicer was Trump’s first press secretary.
Spicer defended Zacharia against some criticism of her debut, arguing that she had been given insufficient preparation time.
- Josh Earnest — Barack Obama, 2014–2017. An Obama campaign communications aide, Earnest worked as a deputy in the White House press office before becoming its leader.
- Jay Carney — Obama, 2011–2014. A former Time magazine journalist, Carney served as Biden’s vice-presidential communications director before succeeding Robert Gibbs.
- Robert Gibbs — Obama, 2009–2011. A longtime Obama adviser and campaign spokesman, Gibbs later became McDonald’s global chief communications officer.
An office shaped by television, crisis and presidential access
The modern position dates to 1929, when Herbert Hoover appointed George Akerson. According to the White House Historical Association, presidential communication changed substantially in 1955, when Dwight Eisenhower’s press secretary, James Hagerty, permitted broadcast equipment to record presidential news conferences. John F. Kennedy held the first live televised presidential news conference in January 1961.
Dee Dee Myers became the first woman to serve as White House press secretary under Bill Clinton in 1993. Another officeholder, James Brady, suffered devastating injuries during the March 1981 assassination attempt on Ronald Reagan. Larry Speakes subsequently assumed the office’s daily duties; Brady’s name is now attached to the briefing room.
Who could come next?
No successor was identified in the dismissal reporting available on October 16.
Before Zacharia’s appointment, CNN conservative commentator Scott Jennings was among the names publicly discussed. Other names circulated in media coverage, but a confirmed White House shortlist or documented sequence of offers has not been established. Jennings’s appearance in that coverage does not establish that he was offered the job.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Drops White House Bombshell: Katie Zacharia Fired After Just Five Days
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has lost another high-profile White House aide, and this time, the departure came almost as quickly as the appointment. Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary just five days after taking the job, bringing an abrupt end to a tenure eclipsed by questions about her qualifications, a poorly received debut briefing, and an extraordinary public intervention from Trump.
A White House official confirmed her dismissal on Friday, October 16, according to The Guardian. The New York Times also reported that she had been fired, while Fox News described her departure as a transition out of the position. The news came hours after Trump told reporters that he had encouraged Zacharia to reconsider whether she wanted to remain in the job.
“I think you’re better off being happy,” Trump recalled telling his newly appointed spokeswoman, suggesting that the intense pressure surrounding her first week might not be worth enduring. The remark immediately raised questions about Zacharia’s future. By Friday afternoon, the uncertainty was over: she was out.
Donald Trump’s warning came just hours before the firing
The speed of Zacharia’s departure makes the episode one of the most remarkable personnel reversals of Trump’s presidency. The White House offered her the position on October 9, replacing Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August.
Zacharia officially began work on Monday, October 12, and delivered her first White House press briefing the following day. Within days, her performance and professional background were attracting scrutiny.
Speaking outside the White House on Friday, Trump appeared to acknowledge the difficulties she was experiencing. He criticized the media’s treatment of her and said he had encouraged her to consider whether the position was right for her.
His comments stopped short of announcing a dismissal, but they hardly amounted to a ringing endorsement. For a press secretary whose authority depends heavily on the president’s confidence, the public hesitation was significant.
Hours later, her departure became public.
The controversy that helped bring down Trump’s newest spokesperson
The most damaging questions about Zacharia focused on her legal credentials. Trump had introduced her as an attorney when announcing her appointment.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school and previously worked in international legal settings. But reports examining her background raised questions about whether she was licensed to practice law.
During a Thursday interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity, Zacharia acknowledged that she had not passed the California bar examination. The revelation augmented scrutiny of her professional background, particularly because her legal qualifications had been highlighted publicly.
Zacharia defended her experience, saying her work involved international transactional law and that she held a law degree. However, graduating from law school does not automatically qualify someone to practice as a licensed attorney.
The distinction became a major issue during her brief time in the White House.
A 14-minute briefing that raised more questions than answers
The questions about Zacharia’s credentials were compounded by criticism of her first appearance before the White House press corps. Her debut briefing on Tuesday lasted approximately 14 minutes.
She took questions from just three organizations: Breitbart News, Fox News and the Daily Mail. The limited exchange prompted complaints that reporters had received little opportunity to question the administration’s newest spokesperson.
The moment was particularly awkward because the White House press secretary is expected to communicate the administration’s positions and respond to questions about government decisions. Zacharia defended her approach and stressed her responsibility to promote the president’s agenda.
But the briefing failed to quiet questions about whether she was prepared for the requirements of the position. Instead, it became the beginning of a week that would finish with her removal.
The White House faces uncomfortable questions of its own
Zacharia’s firing may settle the immediate personnel issue, but it creates a wider problem for the Trump administration. How did a major White House appointment unravel in less than a week?
A press secretary is one of a presidency’s most visible representatives. The position requires communication skills, credibility, preparation, and the faculty to navigate hostile questioning without losing the administration’s message.
Zacharia’s professional background was available for examination before she took the job. That raises legitimate questions about the administration’s vetting process and whether it could have addressed concerns about her credentials before her appointment.
The episode also illustrates a recurring challenge associated with Trump’s management style. The president often makes personnel decisions based on confidence in an individual’s loyalty, communication abilities, and public appeal.
Those qualities can be valuable, but they do not eliminate the need for attentive preparation and scrutiny. Zacharia’s five-day tenure demonstrates how quickly an appointment can become a political distraction when questions emerge immediately after someone assumes a prominent position.
Anthony Scaramucci’s infamous White House record is eclipsed
Zacharia’s extraordinary brevity has already invited comparisons to Anthony Scaramucci. Scaramucci served as White House communications director for just 10 days in 2017 before being dismissed.
His departure became one of the most memorable examples of personnel turmoil during Trump’s first presidency. Zacharia’s exit came after an even shorter period.
Scaramucci responded to the news by admitting that records eventually fall, while expressing sympathy for the difficulties she had experienced. The comparison is especially striking because the two positions, although different, are central to how an administration communicates with the public.
Neither departure is an ordinary staff change. Both illustrate the extraordinary pressures surrounding prominent appointments in Trump’s political operation.
The next press secretary inherits a difficult job
The immediate question is who will replace Zacharia. As of Friday’s initial reporting, the White House had not publicly established a permanent successor.
Whoever takes the position will face the same demanding environment that Zacharia encountered. The administration is approaching the November midterm elections, with political attention increasingly focused on Trump’s policies, economic conditions, and the distribution of power in Congress.
A capable press secretary might assist in maintaining a consistent message during that period. Another prolonged personnel controversy could pull attention away from the issues the administration wants to emphasize.
For Trump, the latest departure presents an uncomfortable contrast. Just days ago, he was celebrating Zacharia’s appointment and displaying confidence that she would succeed. Now, she has been fired before completing her first full week on the job.
The episode is not simply another Washington staffing story. It is a sign that even in a White House dominated by a president who thrives on controlling the headlines, the biggest political distraction can sometimes come from inside his own administration.

The reported dinner suggested that Zacharia’s departure from the press secretary position did not necessarily represent a broader personal break with administration leadership. The report did not establish whether she would receive another government assignment.
Zacharia’s appointment had been announced Oct. 9, with her tenure beginning Monday, Oct. 12. Her selection followed Trump’s decision to replace Leavitt, who had served as a prominent administration spokesperson.
The press secretary position requires daily communication with the White House press corps, coordination with senior administration officials and public explanations of presidential policies and decisions. The role frequently involves questioning on matters ranging from national security and foreign affairs to domestic legislation and executive actions.
Zacharia entered the position with experience as a conservative media commentator and in political communications, but the rapid transition left her facing scrutiny almost immediately.
Her removal after five days makes her tenure one of the shortest in White House press secretary history. The departure also recalls other brief senior communications appointments during Trump’s administrations, including Anthony Scaramucci’s 11-day tenure as White House communications director in 2017.
The circumstances surrounding Zacharia’s appointment have also drawn attention to the administration’s internal personnel process. Reporting indicated that Trump personally selected her, underscoring the president’s direct involvement in choosing officials responsible for communicating his agenda.
The White House has not publicly detailed what led to the final decision beyond acknowledging the transition. While the questions surrounding Zacharia’s bar examination became the most visible controversy, officials have not established whether that issue alone prompted her departure.
Trump’s defense of Zacharia and reports of continuing support from senior administration figures leave open the possibility that she could remain involved in Republican political or government activities outside the press secretary’s office.
For now, her departure creates another leadership change within the White House communications operation as the administration approaches the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Zacharia’s five-day tenure ended almost as quickly as it began, following a public dispute over her professional qualifications and the demands of representing the president before the national press corps.

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia leaves after just days in role
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the role after only a few days.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump indicated he had encouraged her to reconsider her position.
"I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," he told reporters as he departed the White House.
"I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider … think about it. But I would reconsider.'"
Ms Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Mr Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.
Ms Zacharia had got off to a rocky start with her debut press room briefing on Tuesday morning, local time.
It lasted less than 15 minutes, beginning with a remarkably slow reading of what she said were Mr Trump's many accomplishments, before she took just three questions from journalists.
According to two separate White House officials, Ms Zacharia has been "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position.
Speaking to Fox News on Friday, Mr Trump said he was in no rush to name a new press secretary.
Credentials questioned
She was then plunged into controversy when it emerged that her earlier claims of being a lawyer were false.
Ms Zacharia has long described herself as a lawyer, while working to establish herself as a commentator for conservative outlets like Fox News and Newsmax.
But so far, neither she nor the White House have provided evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.
The questions have added to the confusion surrounding Mr Trump's decision to hire Ms Zacharia, who had worked for his social media company for only a few months when he announced her appointment.
Ms Zacharia's credentials were further questioned when she appeared on conservative media outlet Real America's Voice.

sources.text:
Katie Zacharia has had a rough week. Rather than defending President Trump and his policies, the new White House press secretary spent the past few days defending her performance at Tuesday’s embarrassing 14-minute press conference and struggling to explain why she’s been identifying herself as a lawyer despite failing the bar exam. Then, she was summarily shown the door.
Zacharia’s attempts to defend herself on Hannity and Fox & Friends were so disastrous that by Friday afternoon, Trump told the media he’d opened the door for her to exit, saying he told her, “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider” staying in the job.
Sure enough, less than an hour later, the New York Times reported that Zacharia had been fired.
Zacharia’s troubles began hours before Tuesday’s White House debut, when independent journalist Judd Legum reported that there was no evidence that the new press secretary — who President Trump had called an “attorney” — passed the bar exam. When reporters asked what state she passed the bar in, Zacharia gave the bufuddling answer, “When I moved to China.” The Wall Street Journal reported that she actually failed the California bar exam in 2011 and never retook it. Zacharia told the New York Times that an unnamed president of Pepperdine University, where she attended law school, told her it was okay to call herself a “lawyer,” but not an “attorney.”
This defense started unraveling immediately. “Lawyer” might have a little more wiggle room than “attorney,” but there’s considerable disagreement. As the Times put it: “Many legal experts have said this week that because [Zacharia] does not have a license to practice law, she is neither.” The outlet reached out to two recent Pepperdine presidents and neither would take responsibility for giving Zacharia the go-ahead to be a “lawyer.”
Clearly Zacharia needed to pivot to some more sympathetic outlets. She started out as Trump-friendly as possible, elaborating on her decision to not retake the bar in a Thursday afternoon interview with Real America’s Voice’s Jack Posobiec. The MAGA influencer and conspiracy theorist didn’t really push Zacharia, but the headline that emerged from their chat was that Zacharia saw the bar results as “somewhat inconsequential”:
A few hours later, Zacharia’s lawyer vs. attorney distinction took a hit when CNN reported that she’d shared more than a dozen social media posts identifying herself as the latter.
Good thing she was about to sit down with President Trump’s good friend Sean Hannity! Or not. The Fox News host’s Thursday night interview with Zacharia was stunningly brutal.
He began by unsympathetically recapping her awful week and asking, “What happened?” Zacharia said she’d only been offered the job days ago, and felt she “really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference with very little prep time.”
Hannity didn’t seem to buy that excuse. He responded, “Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?”
Then he asked about the CNN report, and got this garbled response: “I think they were retweets and I corrected the record and said that’s not endorsing the title, they were retweets of a title that had been given.”
Hannity opined that the press secretary shouldn’t have gotten into “this long drawn out” explanation of a lawyer versus an attorney because, “most people don’t see much of a distinction.”
He closed by asking, “Why only three questions in 14 minutes, and what might you do a little differently going forward?” Then exit music played over Zacharia’s response.
Many noted that Hannity almost never grills Trump officials like this, and the president was almost certainly watching:
Zacharia got one more shot to smooth things over on Friday morning when she called in to Fox & Friends. But that went awfully too. After one softball opening question, host Lawrence Jones noted it’s been a “tough week,” and asked, “Do you wish you would have disclosed to the president about the bar and not passing the bar?”
“Those questions weren’t asked,” she said. “I’m being hired as white house Press secretary not White House counsel.”
The rest of the interview didn’t go any better. Zacharia seemed unprepared to discuss the Trump administration’s efforts to deport Representative Ilhan Omar, and Lawrence closed by asking, “Katie, it’s a tough question, do you think you still have the confidence of the president?”
Had the press secretary stayed on, next week probably wouldn’t have been any easier. On Friday, National Review’s Jim Geraghty started asking questions about her husband Tyler Zacharia’s work in North Korea:
While her time at the White House was brief, at least the press secretary left her mark; from now on we can measure embarrassingly short White House stints in Zacharias, not Scaramuccis.

The chaotic nature of Zacharia's appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president's first term, which had largely been absent from his second. In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press. “I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,'” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’” Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House did not respond to a request for confirmation. Zacharia plans to have dinner with Vice President JD Vance and his family on Friday evening, according to another person with knowledge of the meal who was granted anonymity to disclose it. In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, "'Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and that he wanted "her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.” The president said he’d make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, “When I get back, we’re gonna talk.” He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job. Zacharia's first official day on the job was Monday In Zacharia's first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes. Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand. She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings. In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also wouldn't say when her next press briefing might be. Questions about why Zacharia called herself a lawyer Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China. That was part of the unusual amount of skepticism that Zacharia faced from those friendly to the administration, including Fox News host Sean Hannity, who pressed the new White House spokeswoman on why she wasn’t forthcoming about her professional background. Hannity, known to be friendly with Trump, asked Zacharia after she confirmed she did not pass the bar exam in California, “Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine law school and then took a different career path and I took the bar once and didn’t pass it?’” “Why get into this long, drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?" he asked. "Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction. Why didn’t you just say, ‘I never practiced law?’" Zacharia reiterated to Hannity that she wasn't acting as a lawyer nor offering legal advice. And she said Friday during that Fox News interview that she wasn’t asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary. Both she and Trump have said she was hired to work in press and communications, not as an administration lawyer. Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president’s social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration. ___ Price reported from Dobbins Air Force Base, Georgia.

EasyJet and Ryanair have announced cuts to their winter schedule rather than run loss-making flights.
Mike Malik, chief industry officer at Cirium aviation, said smaller airports would be hit hardest.

Trump told reporters on Friday that he urged Zacharia to rethink the job. “I just spoke to her about it. I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?’ Because she’s been treated very rough, and she’s a nice person,” he said.
“I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it. But I would reconsider’. She’s got a beautiful husband and family. I said, ‘You should reconsider because you don’t want to go through this’.”
Trump said he would let Zacharia make the decision. However, his remarks left little possibility she could continue in the role. “Maybe it’s not for her,” he said of the high-pressure position.
Minutes after Trump made the remarks while departing the White House, several US news outlets including CNN and The New York Times reported that Zacharia had been fired, citing people familiar with the matter.
Zacharia did not accompany Trump as he left the White House for a rally in Georgia on Friday. Communications director Steven Cheung was present on the South Lawn instead as the president took questions from reporters.
The 41-year-old Zacharia’s first week in the highly scrutinised role included unusually combative interviews on Fox News on Thursday night and Friday morning, both of which Trump watched.
Anchors Sean Hannity and Lawrence Jones separately grilled Zacharia over her legal qualifications and why she had not told Trump she never passed the bar.
“Those questions weren’t asked,” she told Jones.
Zacharia also explained that she was only offered the job last Wednesday, flew to Washington and attended a meeting at the White House on Friday, flew home to California on Saturday and then back to Washington on Sunday before starting in the job on Monday and briefing the press on Tuesday morning.
“What I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference with very little prep time,” she told Hannity. “I received briefing materials in the morning of Tuesday.”
The “tough” Fox News interviews were widely seen as orchestrated tests for Zacharia and setups to justify her removal by the president.
Her five-day tenure sets a record for the shortest-lived White House press secretary in US history, beating the 11 days served by Anthony Scaramucci during the first Trump administration.
“Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain,” Scaramucci posted on Friday.
He said to Zacharia: “Speaking as the world’s leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realise that the Universe did you a major favour.”
Zacharia replaced former press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August to focus on her family after giving birth to her second child in May.
Leavitt had only been back in the role briefly after her maternity leave. The White House has been without a regular press secretary for months in 2026, and the role is now vacant again just weeks before the midterm elections.
Meanwhile, Trump emphatically rejected reports that he is considering replacing his chief-of-staff Susie Wiles. Politico reported this week that the president was sounding out allies about possible replacements, and that he “blew up” when aide Natalie Harp printed out Politico’s stories for him.
“That’s a false report,” Trump said on Friday. “I could not be more happy with Susie. She’s done a great job from day one. She’s been fantastic … That story is a total fake story. We told them that before they wrote it.”

Trump Fires His New Press Secretary After Disastrous First Week
sources.text:
President Donald Trump fired Katie Zacharia from her post as White House press secretary after less than a week on the job, according to a source familiar with the matter.
It’s a stunning exit for Zacharia, who had been beleaguered by bad headlines and questions about her qualifications from the start of her five-day tenure.
Though it happened quickly, many officials both inside and outside the White House were bracing for Zacharia to either be relieved of her position or phased out slowly, according to multiple people The Washington Sun spoke with.
“It takes a certain skill set that she, as a television personality, doesn’t have,” said one Republican close to Trump who has spoken to him recently.
Trending
Another MAGA ally said they had an X post drafted, ready to mark goodbye and good luck to the president’s latest hire after conversations with officials on Friday and Zacharia’s recent interviews.
The mood inside the press office at the White House has seemed bleak, according to a third person familiar with the office, as junior press aides dealt with a deluge of negative headlines about Zacharia and questions over how long she would remain their boss.
Trump foreshadowed the exit on Friday, telling reporters that he asked her to consider stepping aside after a difficult first week on the job.
“Katie has been treated very badly by the media. Very, very badly. Very unfair,” Trump said. “I just asked her, is this for you? And she’s a nice person. I’m going to let her make that decision.”
When asked whether she would remain in the administration if ousted, Trump replied, “In some form.”
“But maybe a more pleasant form,” he added.
There were few signs it would be Zacharia’s last day on the job Friday morning.
When she arrived at the White House, she walked up to reporters and told them she was looking forward to working with them, adding that she would not be taking any questions.
She also appeared on “Fox and Friends” to discuss her new role, telling the hosts she “hit the ground running” and went to Alaska, Montana and Arizona with Trump following her first briefing.
Lawrence Jones, one of the show’s hosts, asked her if she wished she’d disclosed to the president that she hadn’t passed the bar.
“Those questions weren’t asked,” Zacharia said. “I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel. The reason I was hired was to represent the president in the press.”
Trump announced her appointment in a Truth Social post last Friday, and she assumed the position on Monday.
Asked for comment, the White House sent a statement from communications director Steven Cheung: “You guys were better as NOTUS.”
The president didn’t consult his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, on his replacement for Karoline Leavitt, two people told The Sun, hiring Zacharia quickly after a meeting inside the Oval Office. And it was unclear what form of vetting, if any, took place.
A White House official pushed back on this assessment, telling The Sun that Wiles was aware and briefed. They also slammed those speculating about staffers’ moods, saying those people “simply are not in the know and have no clue about what is going on.”
The situation careened off the rails after Zacharia’s first press conference, widely panned for its brevity (15 minutes), the opening statement (which took eight minutes) and the lack of questions from reporters.
Seeking to reset, Zacharia then participated in a series of awkward interviews on friendly networks like Fox News and Real America’s Voice, which still left the president and his allies questioning her ability to perform the strenuous job of speaking for the commander-in-chief.
The press office has been without a press secretary since August after Leavitt left the post, a decision she said was made to spend more time with her family. Since then, White House communications director Steven Cheung has been running the operation. Cheung, not Zacharia, appeared next to the president Friday when he was talking to reporters. Danielle Alvarez, a senior adviser from Trump’s 2024 campaign, has also been spotted with the president and has signed multiple statements as White House spokesperson, though no official announcement of a new role was made.
Officials had said that Trump was in no rush to name a replacement for Leavitt, but the president has taken to openly questioning whether his administration’s wins are being effectively communicated to the public — a knock against his communications operation amid a deluge of difficult headlines. Trump told close advisers he would prefer a man to fill Karoline Leavitt’s position, The Sun reported in August.
Still, Zacharia’s hire presented a new beginning for the press team, even if many had not worked with her before.
Fox News was the first of multiple outlets to report her ouster following Trump’s comments.
Trump didn’t drop names when asked who her successor could be, but he told a reporter: “A lot of people want the job. I bet you’d want it if I offered it to you.”
Controversy surrounding Zacharia’s legal credentials became a focal point this week after Popular Information reported that Zacharia, a California resident, has never been admitted to practice law in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia.
Zacharia herself confirmed she hadn’t passed the bar in a viral interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity.
“You took the bar exam but you didn’t pass the bar exam, correct?” Hannity asked her.
“Yes, Sean,” she answered. Hannity then asked her if she took the bar a second time, and she responded she did not.
Despite this, Zacharia repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer when appearing on podcasts and on TV. Zacharia told The New York Times she decided to publicly refer to herself as an attorney after consulting with Pepperdine University’s president.
The university president warned her not to use the words “attorney” or “esquire,” but said “lawyer” was permissible, the Times reported.
On her LinkedIn page, Zacharia also identified herself as former general counsel to Fix California, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting conservative values across the state, and as a former associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013.
The Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California State Bar on Wednesday over allegations that Zacharia had misrepresented herself as an attorney, a criminal offense punishable by up to one year in a county jail or a fine of up to $1,000, the complaint says.
As the music played out on Hannity, Zacharia continued trying to assure the host she’d deliver for the president.
“I’ll be very prepared, Sean, and I’ll step up to the duty … as press secretary.”
The morning after her Hannity interview, a former Trump official sent The Washington Sun a link to a Polymarket X post, unprompted and without context. Zacharia’s odds to be fired had increased by 12%.
“The final straw wasn’t Hannity. The final straw was lying to The Boss,” the former official texted, referring to the confusion over Zacharia’s legal credentials.
A current administration official only had one word for her performance with the typically friendly Hannity: “Wow.” He continued: “Let’s get someone serious now.”

Katie Zacharia has been fired as White House press secretary after less than one week on the job, The New York Times reported Friday, citing three anonymous sources. She hosted one 14-minute press briefing, took 3 questions, and will go down in history as the press secretary with the shortest tenure to date.
Fox News also reported that Zacharia would be “transitioning out” of the job, though it’s unclear what exactly that means.
Zacharia has faced intense media scrutiny and blowback this week regarding her bogus legal credentials, train-wreck first press briefing, and a disastrous appearance on Fox News’s Hannity where she tried to defend calling herself a “lawyer” but not an “attorney.”
The news of her exit comes shortly after President Donald Trump told reporters that the media was treating Zacharia “nastily” but admitted he had suggested she “reconsider” the position.
“I said, ‘Katie, you don’t have do this if you don’t wanna.’ She said, ‘This is a lot tougher.’ I said, ‘Welcome to the world of Trump.’”
“Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,” the president said he told her.
“I said to her, honestly if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.”
CNN White House reporter Kaitlan Collins reported that Trump was “embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia’s briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance.”
“The main reason he rushed to select her after growing irritated with how long the process was taking to replace Karoline Leavitt was because he wanted more people defending him on TV,” Collins added. “When she failed to do so in a sufficient way with Sean Hannity, Trump said he knew she needed to go.”
Zacharia has spent much of her five days as press secretary attempting to justify calling herself a “lawyer,” despite never having passed the bar exam. She may face investigation in the state of California for purportedly calling herself a “lawyer” without a license after a bar complaint was filed Wednesday.
“Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain,” ex–Trump communications director Antony Scaramucci wrote on X following Zacharia’s termination. Scaramucci stood behind the White House briefing room podium in Trump’s first term for a then-record 11 days, from July 21 to July 31, 2017. Zacharia lasted about 0.4 percent of that time.

Rudy Giuliani’s legal defense fund has spent $1.2 million throughout the 2026 election cycle—but the vast majority of it hasn’t gone to legal fees.
